content: The pooled sensitivity and specificity of diagnostic tests for tuberculosis (TB) were analyzed across various studies and settings. The sensitivity and specificity values are presented with 95% credible intervals (CrI), reflecting the range of uncertainty in the estimates. 1. Overall Accuracy: Across 8 studies involving 3,449 participants, the pooled sensitivity was 42% (31–55%), and the specificity was 91% (85–95%). In 7 studies with 3,365 participants, the sensitivity was 35% (22–50%), and the specificity was 95% (89–98%). 2. By Setting: Inpatient Settings: In 6 studies with 2,253 participants, the sensitivity was 52% (40–64%), and the specificity was 87% (78–93%). In 3 studies with 537 participants, the sensitivity was 62% (41–83%), and the specificity was 84% (48–96%). Outpatient Settings: In 4 studies with 1,196 participants, the sensitivity was 29% (17–47%), and the specificity was 96% (91–99%). In 6 studies with 2,828 participants, the sensitivity was 31% (18–47%), and the specificity was 95% (87–99%). 3. By CD4 Cell Count: CD4 > 200: In 3 studies with 738 participants, the sensitivity was 16% (8–31%), and the specificity was 94% (81–97%). In 1 study with 156 participants, the sensitivity was 27% (6–61%), and the specificity was 99% (96–100%). CD4 ≤ 200: In 4 studies with 1,825 participants, the sensitivity was 45% (31–61%), and the specificity was 89% (77–94%). In 2 studies with 706 participants, the sensitivity was 26% (9–56%), and the specificity was 96% (87–98%). CD4 > 100: In 4 studies with 1,519 participants, the sensitivity was 17% (10–27%), and the specificity was 95% (89–98%). In 4 studies with 952 participants, the sensitivity was 20% (10–35%), and the specificity was 98% (95–99%). CD4 ≤ 100: In 4 studies with 1,239 participants, the sensitivity was 54% (38–69%), and the specificity was 88% (77–94%). In 3 studies with 417 participants, the sensitivity was 47% (40–64%), and the specificity was 90% (77–96%). CD4 101–200: In 4 studies with 586 participants, the sensitivity was 24% (14–38%), and the specificity was 90% (77–96%). In 1 study with 103 participants, the sensitivity was 38% (14–68%), and the specificity was 99% (94–100%). 4. By CD4 and Setting: CD4 ≤ 200 in Inpatients: In 2 studies with 1,009 participants, the sensitivity was 54% (34–73%), and the specificity was 80% (58–91%). In 1 study with 54 participants, the sensitivity was 64% (35–87%), and the specificity was 82% (67–93%). CD4 ≤ 100 in Inpatients: In 2 studies with 734 participants, the sensitivity was 61% (40–78%), and the specificity was 81% (61–91%). In 2 studies with 200 participants, the sensitivity was 57% (33–79%), and the specificity was 90% (69–97%). CD4 101–200 in Inpatients: In 2 studies with 275 participants, the sensitivity was 32% (16–57%), and the specificity was 81% (55–92%). In 1 study with 9 participants, the sensitivity was 44%, but specificity was not applicable. CD4 ≤ 200 in Outpatients: In 1 study with 249 participants, the sensitivity was 24% (16–33%), and the specificity was 94% (89–97%). In 2 studies with 652 participants, the sensitivity was 21% (8–48%), and the specificity was 96% (89–99%). CD4 ≤ 100 in Outpatients: In 1 study with 121 participants, the sensitivity was 30% (18–46%), and the specificity was 93% (85–98%). In 2 studies with 217 participants, the sensitivity was 40% (20–64%), and the specificity was 87% (68–94%). CD4 101–200 in Outpatients: In 1 study with 128 participants, the sensitivity was 18% (8–31%), and the specificity was 95% (87–99%). In 1 study with 94 participants, the sensitivity was 22% (3–60%), and the specificity was 99% (94–100%). 5. WHO Guidelines on TB and HIV: TB patients living with HIV should receive the same duration of daily TB treatment as HIV-negative TB patients. This is a strong recommendation with high certainty of evidence. For individuals with TB and histoplasmosis co-infection, TB therapy should follow WHO guidelines. This is a conditional recommendation based on very low certainty evidence. Early initiation of TB treatment and antiretroviral therapy (ART) is critical for reducing mortality and improving TB treatment outcomes in people with TB and HIV. Preventive TB treatment (TPT) is recommended for all adults and adolescents living with HIV who are unlikely to have active TB. This includes those on ART, pregnant women, and individuals previously treated for TB, regardless of immune suppression or latent TB infection (LTBI) testing availability. 6. Preventive TB Treatment Regimens: Recommended regimens include 6 or 9 months of daily isoniazid, a 3-month regimen of weekly rifapentine plus isoniazid, or a 3-month regimen of daily isoniazid plus rifampicin. These are strong recommendations with moderate to high certainty of evidence. In high TB transmission settings, daily isoniazid preventive treatment (IPT) for at least 36 months is conditionally recommended, regardless of ART status or immune suppression. 7. Pregnancy and TB Prevention: Pregnant women living with HIV are at increased risk of TB, which can have severe consequences for both mother and fetus. Preventive treatment with isoniazid and rifampicin, which are generally considered safe during pregnancy, is recommended. 8. Integrated Care for TB and HIV: Delivering ART in TB treatment settings has been shown to increase ART uptake and timeliness. However, data on mortality and TB treatment success are inconsistent. Providing TB treatment in HIV care settings has shown comparable TB treatment success rates and ART uptake. 9. Drug-Drug Interactions: Co-occurrence of TB and histoplasmosis can complicate management due to drug-drug interactions, particularly between rifampicin and itraconazole. Adjustments to treatment regimens, such as increasing itraconazole doses or replacing rifampicin with rifabutin, may be necessary. 10. Testing for TB Infection: Either the tuberculin skin test (TST) or interferon-gamma release assays (IGRAs) can be used to test for TB infection. Mycobacterium tuberculosis antigen-based skin tests (TBSTs) are also an option. These findings and recommendations emphasize the importance of tailored diagnostic and treatment strategies for TB in people living with HIV, considering their unique clinical and immunological profiles.
